specialised-analyses.title: Structural variants, repeats, Paraphase and mtDNA
specialised-analyses.summary: The analyses beyond small variants, including the CNV classifier and the variant summary.
paragraphs: The Structural variants page opens on the Mendeliome panel, with a population frequency below 1% and the affected members as carriers. Its filters sit under Advanced filters, closed when the page opens and laid out as on the small-variant page: Phenotype, Inheritance and support, Locations, Class and breakpoints, Needlr annotations and Review; the presets are Mendeliome, Dominant, Recessive-like and Any affected. Phenotype prioritization ranks SVs by the same phenotype score as small variants, and Rank by Variant score orders them by the variant score alone, as on the small-variant page. Clear all filters removes the default.

Save current keeps your filters as a saved search: for this family, or, with Every family I open (reusable), for each family you open. Your saved searches are listed under the presets. Choose one and Delete saved search removes it; a reusable one goes from every family.

As on the small-variant page, a gene panel of any size keeps an SV whose annotation names one of its genes or that overlaps one of its regions. So the Mendeliome also keeps an SV in one of its genes whose annotation names that gene otherwise, and a small panel an SV annotated with one of its genes that does not overlap it, such as a gene a few kilobases away. With both a gene panel and a Gene symbol filled in, an SV must meet both.

The classification under Review keeps an SV by the class its review shows, as on the small-variant page. A class word typed as the classification (VUS) gives its class; otherwise the review's class tag gives it, the most severe of two; otherwise the classification as typed. A CNV classification counts with the class it saved as the classification. So Likely pathogenic - class 4 also finds an SV classified by its class tag alone, and not one classified as VUS - class 3 beside the Pathogenic - class 5 tag: that SV shows class 5. Capitals do not matter.

A row or card shows its review's class once, by that rule, as on the small-variant page. A class tag of another class is not shown beside it; the VUS tiers and Secondary finding are tags, never the class. Download CSV exports the list: its Classification column holds the class shown, Classification text the classification as typed, and Tags the review's tags.
Min length and Exact length, under Class and breakpoints, measure an SV by the Length the list shows, without a deletion's minus sign. That length is:

An insertion is as long as the sequence it inserts, although most callers write its end at its start. A length typed with a minus sign, as the list writes a deletion's, is read without it. A translocation (BND, TRA) has no length: the list shows none, every minimum keeps it, and no exact length finds it.

A filtered search reads at most 50,000 SVs of the callset before it applies the filters. With Phenotype prioritization on (the default) it ranks at most 5,000 of the SVs that match. When a search reaches either limit, a warning says "Results may be incomplete" ("Ranking may be incomplete" when the list is ranked), the count shows a +, and an SV beyond the limit is not shown. Narrow the search with a region, a gene panel or a gene. A gene panel of any size (the Mendeliome included) and a gene are applied before the 50,000 are read, so the limit counts only the SVs they keep. The family report's list of reported SVs is not cut by this limit: it reads the reported SVs themselves.
ACMG (CNV) on a row opens the ClinGen copy-number classifier (Riggs et al. 2020): choose Copy-number loss or Copy-number gain, check the pre-selected criteria and add the rest.
The Repeat expansions page lists each repeat locus with every member's call: the repeat count of each allele, and a status read against the locus's thresholds in the repeat catalogue (STRchive):

The cutoffs are STRchive's thresholds for the locus, as STRchive states them. STRchive, beside IGV, Chromosome view and OMIM on a locus's card, opens the locus's page on STRchive: its disease, ranges, motifs and references.

Aberrant only, ticked when the page opens, keeps every locus whose status is not Normal or Unknown, Not assessed included. The page header counts the calls not assessed. This page and the genome tracks classify every call again, against the catalogue as it is now, and the tracks colour each call by the status the repeat page gives it.
Near a boundary. TRGT counts the motif across the region its own catalogue gives a locus, which need not be the clinical repeat number the locus's ranges count:

So at every locus a count within 3 repeats of a boundary the locus's classification uses is marked Near a boundary beside its call. Hover over or focus the mark for the count, the nearest count on each side that reads another status, and what is known of TRGT's count at the gene. The status itself is not changed: read the call with the mark in mind. Aberrant only keeps such a locus whatever its status, the page header counts the calls near a boundary, and a genome track says it in the locus's tooltip.
Count correction. QA can have a correction recorded for a locus, in repeats, with a reason: an administrator enters it on the admin page Repeat catalogue. No locus has one until QA enters it.

Some genes lie in regions with nearly identical copies, such as SMN1/SMN2 or PMS2, where standard variant calling fails. The Paraphase page shows, per locus, what Paraphase found there for each member: the copy number, and a status read from a catalogue of medical regions.

Copy-number changes and abnormal calls only, ticked when the page opens, shows the regions with such a change or with a member's call that reads Pathogenic, Carrier or Review: a fusion, or an RCCX allele that is not normal, is reviewed without any change in copy number. Untick it to see every region.

Each card leads to the region's genes. A region of one gene links its name to the gene page, SMN1/SMN2 links each gene in its name, and the RCCX module links CYP21A2, TNXB, C4A and C4B under Genes. How to read opens, under the card, what the region is and how its calls read: what Normal, Carrier and Pathogenic mean there, the caveat, and what each copy number and extra field holds. For the RCCX module it adds how the module is built, Paraphase's allele labels, the CYP21A2 variant names with the form of CAH each usually gives, what failed phasing means, TNXB and C4; for the CFH gene cluster, how its two segments lie and which genes a fusion in each removes. The guide explains; it calls nothing. Extra info shows each member's technical readout, a list one item per line, such as one RCCX allele per chromosome.

Each repeat locus and Paraphase region has its own review, kept per family and reference assembly. Its card has the controls of every variant card: Review, Exclude and Report toggle their tag, and Tags & notes opens the review. There you give your classification on the type's own scale, beside CoGA's status, which it never changes:

The ACMG class tags and VUS tiers are for small variants and are not offered here. A review that already holds one lists it, marked, so you can untick it. The card shows your classification as Review: …. It adds Differs from CoGA's status when the classification agrees with none of the members' calls (a Normal where every call reads Pathogenic, say). A review is of the locus or region, so a classification that fits one member's call is not marked. Exclude folds the card to its heading; the card stays in the list, Aberrant only included.

CoGA freezes the calls a classification, or the Report tag, rests on when you save it. When the calls change after that (a new import, a count correction QA recorded), the card says Changed since review, and the tooltip names what changed. It says No call since review when the family holds no call there any more. A save of tags or a note alone keeps the calls your classification rests on. Sign-out checks them again (see Clinical report).

On the mtDNA analysis page, each sample's row in the family summary gives its mean chrM depth, the share of chrM covered, and a QC status judged against the lab's limits (Sequencing QC thresholds). The depth comes from one coverage track that holds read depth: the sample's coverage BED when it was declared as read depth, otherwise HiFiCNV's depth where the import stored it as read. These never count: WisecondorX's and QDNAseq's bins, HiFiCNV's normalised depth and a coverage BED declared as a log2 ratio (they hold log2 ratios, not depths), and a coverage BED that does not say what it holds. A sample without a track of read depth shows the depth of its chrM calls, and the page's QC notes name each track left out and why.

Each mtDNA variant has the same review as a small variant, and its card the same controls: Review, Exclude, Report, Tags & notes and ACMG classify. It is one review: the same variant on the Small variants page shows the same tags and note, and Report puts it on the report with the other reported small variants. ACMG classify on a variant from the mtDNA analysis page uses the mitochondrial rule set.

A card links to IGV, the chromosome view, OMIM (for a variant in a gene), MITOMAP and VarSome. VarSome opens the variant on the revised Cambridge Reference Sequence, whatever the family's assembly. A single-base change that alters the protein of one of the 13 protein-coding genes also links to MitImpact, which holds only such changes.

Variant summary, the last link of the family's analyses, describes all the variant data the family holds. It is shown when the family has any. A row of tabs at the top has one tab per kind of data the family has, and the page shows one kind at a time: the first tab opens, and a click on another shows that kind instead. The figures describe the calls. No filter, classification or sign-out reads them.
A tab loads when you first open it, and keeps its figures when you switch away and back. One that could not be loaded says so and offers Retry; the other tabs still work.

Exploratory — not for clinical use. The Ancestry (exploratory) section, at the end of a family's Sample QC, places its individuals beside public reference populations on four principal components: genetic similarity, not an ancestry percentage or an ethnic identity. It is outside CoGA's intended purpose, has not been validated, and is never part of the sign-out or of the signed record. It reads the family's stored GRCh38 callsets, measures whether each covers a genome, an exome or only part of the markers, and is calculated again automatically when the genotypes change. For one individual you can choose another callset, give the regions of a gene panel or a BED file, include an embryo or leave the individual out.
blocks: Filter and review CNVs and other SVs with their genotypes, rank them by phenotype, classify copy-number changes, and tag them for the report.
Per-sample repeat calls, scored against the STRchive catalogue of disease loci.
Genes in paralogous or duplicated regions, where standard variant calling is unreliable.
mtDNA variants and large chrM deletions and duplications, each with its heteroplasmy per member, and each sample's mtDNA coverage.
for a call written as its sequence without an SVLEN (as VCF 4.4 writes one), the bases it inserts or deletes;
otherwise, the end minus the start.

Normal, Grey zone (the intermediate range), Premutation (an FMR1 allele of 55–200 repeats, which can expand in a child) and Pathogenic. Where the catalogue gives a locus a benign range and a pathogenic threshold but no grey zone, a count between the two reads Grey zone: it is neither benign nor pathogenic.
Review: outside catalogued ranges: a count the catalogue cannot classify at a locus that is pathogenic by contraction.
Review: two chrX alleles in a male: a male's call with two different chrX alleles, where he carries one; a note explains it.

Not assessed: a call at a locus without thresholds. No catalogued locus matches its TRID (a locus the catalogue lacks, or a TRID spelled differently), or the catalogue gives the locus no threshold. CoGA cannot say whether such a count is normal; its cutoff reads No reference cutoff. Where the catalogue gives a locus a benign range but no threshold (STRchive's POLG: 10 repeats), a count inside the range reads Normal and any other count Not assessed; the cutoff reads normal 10 · no threshold. The count is the copies TRGT reports of the catalogued motif, in every rotation the call lists (GAA and AAG at FXN), across the whole locus, flanking copies included, so it can run higher than the count the range describes. In the TRGT catalogue in use (TRID CPEO_POLG), POLG's common allele of 10 repeats counts 14 and stays Not assessed.

A gene with several repeat tracts, each a locus of its own in STRchive (ARX, HOXA13), has thresholds per tract. A call whose TRID is the gene's name is read against the tract its region overlaps. If the region overlaps none of the tracts, or more than one, the call reads Not assessed, and its note names the tracts and says why.
at FMR1 it leaves out the AGG interruptions, so an allele reads 1 to 3 below its clinical number (a premutation of 55 repeats can read 53, in the grey zone);
at HTT it also counts the CAG after the CAA interruption, one above the usual count;
at POLG it counts four flanking GCT copies, so the common 10-repeat allele reads 14.

CoGA adds it to TRGT's count before the count is classified. The call shows the corrected count with TRGT's own in brackets, 17 / 36 (TRGT 18 / 37), and the card's Count correction line gives the correction and its reason.
The status, the mark, the genome tracks and the signed record all use the corrected count. A correction does not lift the mark.

Signing out freezes, beside each call, the corrected count, TRGT's own count and the mark, and for each locus QA's record: the correction, the reason, by whom and when. A correction changed after sign-out makes the report say the repeat expansions changed since.
Where the catalogue has a rule for the locus, the copy number reads as Normal, Carrier or Pathogenic, or as Review when it fits none of them.

At a locus without a rule, a copy-number change or a fusion reads as Review. A change is a copy number outside the normal range the catalogue records for the locus (6 for NEB, 4 for a gene with its pseudogene).
On chrX a man has one copy and a woman two, by the sex Paraphase infers, else the pedigree's. Without a sex, a chrX value is not called normal.
A field without a fixed normal value (highest_total_cn) and a no-call are no change.

At the RCCX module CoGA also reads Paraphase's label for each chromosome (annotated_alleles). A label that is not a normal allele, a number of labels other than two, or failed phasing reads as Review, whatever the copy number. CoGA never calls a carrier or an affected person there. Paraphase's own TNXB result, TNXB counted apart from its pseudogene TNXA, has a card of its own.

The CFH gene cluster has three cards: one for each of the two segments Paraphase counts there, CFH cluster segment A and CFH cluster segment B, and one for the cluster as a whole, which holds both segments' fusions. One deletion or duplication shows on more than one of them, each with its own review.
Reviewing a repeat locus or a Paraphase region
a repeat locus: Pathogenic expansion, Reduced penetrance, Premutation, Intermediate (grey zone), Normal or Uncertain significance;
a Paraphase region: Affected, Carrier, Risk allele, Normal or Uncertain significance.

NIPT-M, first, for a monogenic NIPT family: the plasma's sites as the NIPT analysis classes them, with the NIPT page's fetal fraction, filters and categories. The plasma's GT is no genotype (Mutect2 writes 0/1 on every call, and the plasma holds the mother's and the fetus's DNA), so the genotypes come from the allele fractions. The fetal fraction, the sites grouped, the fetal sex, paternity, and what the assay's artefact list did: the alleles removed, how many of the alleles it lists are in this family, and those kept in because ClinVar may call them pathogenic or they are common. An empty list says so. Mother and fetus: the groups one under another, by the mother's genotype and then the fetus's, each with its sites and share, the plasma allele fraction its category predicts beside the median observed, and the share classified with a confidence of 0.99 or more. Each group can be split by the father's genotype or the variant class. Plasma allele fraction, in bins of 0.01. Per group gives each group a row on its own scale, so a small group reads as well as a large one, with a dashed line where its category is expected and a triangle at its observed median. All sites stacks the groups, with numbered lines where the categories are expected; a hom/hom peak far above the rest is cut, its full count beside it, so that the other bins can be read (the log scale shows it whole). Peaks off their lines mean the fetal fraction or the classes do not fit. Hover a bin for its sites. Transmission by chromosome: per autosome, the father's het and hom-alt alleles the fetus inherited, the mother's het alleles, and the fetus's hom-alt sites. An autosome where none of a parent's alleles reached the fetus over at least 20 sites is marked: it can point to uniparental disomy or a deletion. CoGA does not call UPD. Calls and the father's genotypes: the plasma calls through the quality filter and the artefact list, the caller's own FILTER (Mutect2's somatic filters flag many germline calls; the analysis does not use them) and the father's genotype from his allele fraction.

The fetal fraction, the sites grouped, the fetal sex, paternity, and what the assay's artefact list did: the alleles removed, how many of the alleles it lists are in this family, and those kept in because ClinVar may call them pathogenic or they are common. An empty list says so.

Mother and fetus: the groups one under another, by the mother's genotype and then the fetus's, each with its sites and share, the plasma allele fraction its category predicts beside the median observed, and the share classified with a confidence of 0.99 or more. Each group can be split by the father's genotype or the variant class.

Plasma allele fraction, in bins of 0.01. Per group gives each group a row on its own scale, so a small group reads as well as a large one, with a dashed line where its category is expected and a triangle at its observed median. All sites stacks the groups, with numbered lines where the categories are expected; a hom/hom peak far above the rest is cut, its full count beside it, so that the other bins can be read (the log scale shows it whole). Peaks off their lines mean the fetal fraction or the classes do not fit. Hover a bin for its sites.

Transmission by chromosome: per autosome, the father's het and hom-alt alleles the fetus inherited, the mother's het alleles, and the fetus's hom-alt sites. An autosome where none of a parent's alleles reached the fetus over at least 20 sites is marked: it can point to uniparental disomy or a deletion. CoGA does not call UPD.

Calls and the father's genotypes: the plasma calls through the quality filter and the artefact list, the caller's own FILTER (Mutect2's somatic filters flag many germline calls; the analysis does not use them) and the father's genotype from his allele fraction.

Small variants (SNV/indel), counted from the family's own callsets. Imputed genotypes (GLIMPSE2) and chrM are left out; chrM is under mtDNA. Each variant counts once, even when two callsets hold it. In a monogenic NIPT family the plasma's and the father's heterozygous and homozygous counts are left out (their GT is no genotype): the NIPT-M tab classes them. Per sample: variants, heterozygous and homozygous, the het/hom ratio, SNVs, insertions, deletions and other changes, the transition/transversion ratio, and the share that passed the caller's FILTER. Consequences: each variant under its most severe consequence over all its transcripts, in the groups of the small-variant filter, with the total in the coding sequence. The small-variant search may name another transcript of the same variant. Per chromosome: each member's heterozygous and homozygous variants, and the homozygous share. Call quality: histograms of each member's genotype quality, depth and, for heterozygous calls, allele balance. These count calls, so a variant two callsets hold counts twice. Mendelian inconsistencies: for each child with both parents in the family, per callset and autosome. It counts the sites where all three have a biallelic diploid call, and those no transmission explains: the father's allele missing, the mother's, or from neither parent. Many inconsistencies on one chromosome that all miss one parent's allele can point to uniparental disomy or a deletion. CoGA does not call UPD: confirm it by another method.
Per sample: variants, heterozygous and homozygous, the het/hom ratio, SNVs, insertions, deletions and other changes, the transition/transversion ratio, and the share that passed the caller's FILTER.

Consequences: each variant under its most severe consequence over all its transcripts, in the groups of the small-variant filter, with the total in the coding sequence. The small-variant search may name another transcript of the same variant.
Per chromosome: each member's heterozygous and homozygous variants, and the homozygous share.
Call quality: histograms of each member's genotype quality, depth and, for heterozygous calls, allele balance. These count calls, so a variant two callsets hold counts twice.

Mendelian inconsistencies: for each child with both parents in the family, per callset and autosome. It counts the sites where all three have a biallelic diploid call, and those no transmission explains: the father's allele missing, the mother's, or from neither parent. Many inconsistencies on one chromosome that all miss one parent's allele can point to uniparental disomy or a deletion. CoGA does not call UPD: confirm it by another method.

Structural variants, from every caller, HiFiCNV's copy-number calls included: per member and type, per chromosome and type, sharing between members, and length histograms. The WisecondorX and QDNAseq segments are coverage tracks, not variants, and are not counted.
Repeat expansions, Paraphase and Mitochondrial DNA: each member's calls by the status its analysis page gives them, and for mtDNA the haplogroup, the mean depth and the heteroplasmy classes.

visualization.title: Genome visualisation
visualization.summary: From a candidate to its context: the genome and chromosome views, Circos and IGV, and how the small-variant and structural-variant tracks are drawn.
paragraphs: Tables are for finding candidates; viewers are for checking them in their genomic context. From the family page:
The IGV and View links on a variant row or card, and the Genome and Circos buttons above the structural-variant table, open in a new browser tab, so your filtered list stays as it was.
In the chromosome view each small variant is drawn by its class, with a legend on the track:

Any other variant with a conflicting or uncertain ClinVar record is drawn by its impact. The dots differ by colour only: hover a mark for its impact, ClinVar status and parental origin. A review tag draws a ring in the tag's colour around the mark; the mark itself does not change.

In a window of 250 kb or less the track draws every variant of the sample. In a wider window it draws only the variants that are ClinVar pathogenic or likely pathogenic, or of HIGH or MODERATE impact on a transcript and not ClinVar benign or likely benign; its head says so. Zoom in to 250 kb or less to see the others, such as a review-tagged variant of LOW impact. The small-variant list is not affected.

When the sample shown has a parent in the family, the track has three rows: variants inherited from the father (top), from the mother (bottom), and of unknown origin (middle: homozygous, de novo or ambiguous). The origin comes from the parents' genotypes when both are there, otherwise from the phased genotype. Without a parent in the family there is one row.

The chromosome view draws each gene as its preferred transcript (MANE Select, else the Ensembl canonical one, else the longest): exons as blocks, introns as a line with chevrons pointing the way the gene is transcribed (› on the + strand, ‹ on the − strand). Hover a gene for its strand, its transcript and its panels, and, over an exon or an intron, its number in the transcript (Exon 3 / 12), counted from the transcript's start.
Coverage is drawn as one track per CNV caller, on the axis of what the track holds:

In a PGT family, judge each embryo's aneuploidy and large (>10 Mb) structural variants yourself, on its segment, copy-number (coverage) and APCAD tracks. CoGA shows the tracks but makes no aneuploidy call.

For an aneuploidy, tick Parental origin (aneuploidy) under Tracks in the genome and chromosome views. It is offered for an embryo whose PGT pipeline run wrote its segregation table, and is off until you tick it. It draws the embryo's sites as the pipeline's own plots do, in two panels: Mother heterozygous (the pipeline's group 2: the mother heterozygous, the father homozygous) and Father heterozygous (group 3). Each site is at the embryo's allele fraction, from 0 to 1, coloured by the other parent's homozygous allele: amber for the reference (2B, 3B), the heterozygous parent's colour for the alternate (2A, 3A). The genome view draws every chromosome side by side, so an aneuploid one stands out against the others; the chromosome view draws the region in view. Read each panel against its guide lines:
Read the result against the centromere on the chromosome view's ideogram:

The APCAD track shows which parent gave the extra copy of an isodisomic trisomy. The pipeline keeps only sites the embryo was read deeply at, so a trisomic chromosome has many more sites than the others, and a monosomy almost none. CoGA draws the sites and makes no call from them.
The PGT haplotype track is explained under Haplotype segregation.
The genome and chromosome views draw every SV that the structural-variant list shows, in one of six rows:

A CNV is placed by the copy number stored for the sample's call, as the SV ranking scores it: a male has one copy of chrX and chrY outside the pseudo-autosomal regions, and a CNV without a stored copy number counts as a loss. Hover an SV for its type as the caller wrote it, a CNV's copy-number change, and the call's copy number (CN). The Circos plot draws each SV the same way, from the calls of the whole family.
blocks: Genome view — chromosomes 1–22, X and Y with their variants and tracks. The mitochondrion, too small to see there, is in the chromosome view (chrM) and on the mtDNA analysis page.
Chromosome view — one chromosome with coverage, segments, APCAD, haplotypes and variant tracks. Clicking the ROI on the family page opens it here with 1 Mb on each side.
Circos plot — genome-wide structural relationships at a glance, drawn on chromosomes 1–22, X and Y of the family's assembly. For an assembly it cannot draw, the page says why and draws nothing.

IGV viewer — the reads at a locus, on the genome of the family's assembly. For an assembly it has no genome for, the page says so and opens none, rather than another assembly's genome. A sample sequenced short-read and then long-read shows a track of each, named with its analysis. In a family of several analyses every track names its analysis. A recorded alignment whose file is gone shows no track: CoGA never shows another analysis's reads in its place.
ClinVar pathogenic or likely pathogenic, whatever the impact
ClinVar conflicting, with a pathogenic or likely pathogenic classification among them, whatever the impact
LOW or MODIFIER impact, or none

Viewers show only what was imported. A coverage, segment, APCAD or haplotype track appears when that data was loaded for the sample, so an empty track usually means the layer is missing, not that the viewer failed. When a view holds too many variants to draw, the track says so: zoom in or filter.
The callers' log2 ratios share the log2-ratio axis, with the gain and loss colours and the caller's segments. Hover a segment for the values its caller gives (for WisecondorX its z-score).

A conventional NIPT's maternal plasma (ccnv) has an axis of its own (±0.3): a fetal trisomy raises the plasma by only about +0.08 at a 12 % fetal fraction, which the gain and loss colours would never show. Each segment takes the colour of ccnv's call: gain, loss, or purple where ccnv calls it discordant with the fetal fraction (a maternal or mosaic event, say). The dashed lines are where a fetal trisomy (above) and monosomy (below) lie at the plasma's fetal fraction, on chromosomes 1–22 and X. The track's header gives that fetal fraction (ccnv's effective one), the fetal sex and the sex-chromosome call; hover it for every estimate, and a segment for ccnv's values: its call, z-score, bins, expected ratio, implied fetal fraction, discordance and origin.

Read depth is drawn on a depth axis from 0, without those colours or segments. This covers a coverage BED declared as read depth, and a HiFiCNV depth file without autosomal depth: that file gives no baseline to take a ratio against, so its depths are kept as read (the track's header says so).
A coverage BED says what it holds when it is loaded. One that does not is drawn on its own range without an axis, and its header warns that it is read as neither depth nor a log2 ratio.
only ⅓ and ⅔, nothing at 0 or 1
two copies of one of its homologs (isodisomy), or, in a trisomy, the panel of the parent who gave one copy of three
heterodisomy at the centromere points to an error in meiosis I;
isodisomy at the centromere, turning to heterodisomy past a crossover, points to meiosis II;
isodisomy along the whole chromosome points to a mitotic error, usually as a mosaic, where the bands sit between those of a disomy and a trisomy.
Deletions of any subtype (DEL:ME), and CNVs that remove a copy
Duplications of any subtype (DUP:TANDEM), and CNVs that add a copy
Any other type, and CNVs that change no copy number, in grey

haplotype-segregation.title: Haplotype segregation (PGT)
haplotype-segregation.summary: Follow the parental haplotypes through the family to see which embryos inherited the disease haplotype — and when not to trust the call.
paragraphs: The Haplotypes track (chromosome view and genome overview) is CoGA's PGT tool. It colours each person's two haplotypes by the parental homolog they descend from, finds the haplotype that carries the disease allele, and calls each embryo from it.

Each embryo's call is a badge in the Family members table on the family page: Affected / at risk, Carrier, Unaffected or Uninformative. To call an embryo free of a disease haplotype, CoGA needs the embryo's own haplotype across the ROI; without it the embryo reads Uninformative. The server works the calls out from the stored haplotypes. Sign out report freezes the same calls into the signed version (PGT embryo results), each with the haplotypes it rests on, its warnings, its QC at the ROI and that QC's verdict against the thresholds. Next to the badge may be:

Review ROI markers → shows the phased genotypes of every member across the ROI, with each child's Mendelian-error rate. Use it to re-check a surprising call. A single marker that disagrees with its neighbours is noise, not a crossover. A clearly raised Mendelian-error rate points to a swap or a wrong pedigree.
In a single-parent (donor) family the donor lane stays grey, and a recessive call is uninformative because the donor side is unknown.
blocks: Phased imputed genotypes (GLIMPSE2) for the couple, the embryos and the relatives you want coloured.
A correct pedigree, including the grandparents, who anchor the disease haplotype.

Every member's sex, recorded before the phased genotypes are imported. On chrX a man has one X outside the pseudo-autosomal regions, and the haplotypes there are built with the sexes recorded at the import. After recording or correcting a sex, import the phased genotypes again.
Affected and carrier status on the members that define the disease haplotype.

An inheritance model (if none is set, CoGA assumes recessive when a member is marked as a carrier, otherwise dominant) and a region of interest at the disease locus. Without an ROI there are no embryo calls.
P1 and P2 (blues) are the father's homologs, M1 and M2 (greens) the mother's. Untransmitted (grey) is a relative's homolog that was not passed down, or one CoGA could not place.

The lane of the disease haplotype is highlighted: tinted and edged in red, with solid edges (Affected), for a dominant or X-linked model, and in orange, with dashed edges (Carrier), for a recessive one. The band in the lane keeps its homolog's colour. On the genome overview the edges appear only on the ROI's chromosome.

The marker dots are the raw phased markers. Use them to check that a colour change is a real recombination and not phasing noise. They are drawn in a window of 5 Mb or less; in a wider one the track's head says to zoom in.
Next to the track's name, a child's head gives its informative sites in the window. When its Mendelian errors point to a sample swap or a wrong pedigree, it gives them instead, in red.

⚠ phasing QC — the embryo's phasing QC at the ROI does not meet its thresholds, counted over the ROI and 1 Mb on each side: at least 50 informative sites, a Mendelian error rate of at most 2%, and at least 6 markers on each flank of the ROI on each parent's side the call reads. The tooltip names each measure, its value and its threshold. The call stands: check it in the ROI markers before you rely on it. These thresholds are provisional, to be confirmed by the laboratory director and QA. At an X-linked locus a man is counted with his one X: a son against his mother alone.

⚠ both homologs — the embryo's markers at the ROI mix both of a parent's homologs, as where it carries both (a trisomy of that chromosome). Its haplotype blocks show only one of them, so the embryo is not called: it reads Uninformative, and its haplotype tracks show no risk state. The tooltip gives the share of markers off one homolog. Read its copy-number and APCAD tracks. The threshold (more than 10%, over at least 20 markers, on a parent's side the call reads) is provisional too.
⚠ QC not counted — no phasing QC was counted at the ROI, so the call was not checked against the thresholds; the tooltip says why.
⚠ recombination — a haplotype change inside the ROI or within 250 kb of it; the call may not hold across the locus.

⚠ phase corrected — CoGA undid a phase switch in a parent's haplotypes inside or close to the ROI. Where the phase switched is known only roughly, so the call across the locus is less certain: review the ROI markers.
⚠ uninformative — no call is made: no disease haplotype could be resolved, or the embryo's haplotype does not cover the ROI.

⚠ sex unknown — an X-linked recessive call depends on the embryo's sex, which is not recorded. The embryo then reads Affected / at risk or Uninformative, and the warning gives the call for a son and for a daughter. Record the sex to resolve it.

monogenic-nipt.title: Monogenic NIPT
monogenic-nipt.summary: Screen a pregnancy for single-gene disorders from maternal-plasma cfDNA and a paternal sample: set it up, read the page, print the report.
paragraphs: Monogenic NIPT screens a pregnancy for single-gene disorders from cell-free DNA (cfDNA) in maternal plasma, with a sample from the father. The fetus is never sequenced: its genotype is inferred from the cfDNA allele fractions and the fetal fraction (FF), the share of the cfDNA that comes from the fetus.

In Family builder, tick Monogenic NIPT (cfDNA from maternal plasma) and give the Pregnancy ID, the laboratory's ID of the pregnancy. Add the father, the cfDNA sample as the mother (mark it cfDNA (maternal plasma)) and the fetus as the proband: CoGA records it as the pregnancy's fetus (role fetus), which has no data of its own and is neither a proband nor an embryo. A package import does the same when its package says analysis_type: monogenic_nipt and names the pregnancy (pregnancy_id). The family page then shows a Monogenic NIPT button.

The data is the NIPT-M pipeline's output: a single-sample VCF of the plasma and one of the father, with a per-target coverage table for each (coverage_<sample>.txt). The package import finds them by the sample names of the PED. One combined VCF with a father column and a cfDNA column works as well. The calls must carry FORMAT/AD.
A family may hold several pregnancies of one woman. Each pregnancy's NIPT is an analysis of its own: its data, reviews and sign-out are its own.

The built-in presets De novo and Paternal, inherited set a view with high or moderate impact and a gnomAD frequency of 1% or less (a ClinVar pathogenic or likely pathogenic record overrides both); De novo also leaves out ClinVar benign and likely benign. Recessive (both parents carrier) reads the parents as the expanded carrier screen reads a couple: the BeGECS v3 panel, high or moderate impact, a gnomAD frequency below 5% (a ClinVar pathogenic or likely pathogenic record overrides both), ClinVar benign and likely benign left out. The page opens on De novo on the Mendeliome panel, named under the presets as Active filter: De novo, Mendeliome panel (default), as on the small-variant page. Pick a narrower panel if you need one. A link with its own filters, such as Back to NIPT, opens on those.

NIPT report, at the right of the header beside Report, opens a printable summary: the fetal fraction, the quality checks, the coverage of the targets in scope, and the classified variants grouped as De novo in fetus, Dominant, transmitted, Recessive / biallelic risk and Other categories.
Print report prints it.

Sign out NIPT analysis on the NIPT report is the analytical sign-off. It freezes the analysis into a signed record, which the EPD report refers to by its report code. It is the family's own sign-out, with the same checks and report code, whether you sign out here or from the family report. The record holds the NIPT results as CoGA computed them: the pregnancy and its fetuses, the fetal fraction and the quality checks, the coverage, and each variant tagged report with its category, reads, probabilities and recurrence in the other cfDNA samples.

When the family also holds another analysis (the conventional NIPT of the pregnancy, or another pregnancy's NIPT), each is signed out on its own: the NIPT report signs out the monogenic NIPT of the pregnancy it shows, and its record freezes and checks that analysis's data only. The family's Report page signs out the conventional NIPT of each pregnancy.
blocks: A monogenic and a conventional NIPT are one pregnancy only when their packages name the same pregnancy ID. A package of another pregnancy adds an analysis beside the others and changes nothing of theirs.
Each pregnancy has its own plasma and fetus. The father may be the same sample in both: each pregnancy keeps its own copy of his calls.

The NIPT page, its report and the Sample QC show one pregnancy at a time. Choose it in the analysis list beside the family name (monogenic NIPT of pregnancy ZW1). The page opens on the pregnancy imported last.
Two plasmas of one woman, linked as the same individual, are drawn as one person but are never one pregnancy: their results never merge.

When a pregnancy's package lists two or more fetuses, the NIPT page, the NIPT report and the signed version show the multiple-pregnancy note: a fetal result may be present in one fetus or in more than one, and the analysis cannot tell which. The note does not apply to a monozygotic twin, whose fetuses share one genotype; CoGA is not told the zygosity, so it shows the note for every multiple pregnancy.

The header shows the fetal fraction, its 95% confidence interval and the number of sites it rests on, a Low-confidence FF chip when the estimate is weak, and the filter funnel (Total, Quality-filtered, Artifact-filtered, Analysed). As on every family page, it warns Import incomplete while a data import has left the family partly loaded or has not finished, and Not validated for clinical use for a family outside the validated scope.

The diagnostic gene panel says which gene panel the pregnancy's analysis is read and reported within: the indication's panel, or the clinical exome's. Choose it in the card under the header and change it when the indication changes; each change is on the family's audit trail. The page and its report open on it (without one, on the Mendeliome), and the sign-out freezes its version, its gene list and the coverage of its capture targets. A gene of the panel without a capture target is not tested. Without a diagnostic panel the sign-out asks for a reason.

The NIPT report lists the diagnostic candidates of the diagnostic panel by the locked criteria of the R validation (rare, protein-altering, ClinVar read strictly; see the reference): the de novo and paternal alleles the fetus inherited, each of the mother's alleles with the probability that the fetus inherited it, and the recessive genes left for further investigation. The sign-out freezes them with the criteria's version. The page's filters stay adjustable, for exploring.

Quality checks come first: the fetal fraction (with the per-site median and the de novo window), the expected fetal reads, the fetal sex from the father's X alleles and from the chrY coverage, paternity, the maternal plasma sample, the coverage of the capture targets and why cfDNA calls failed the quality filter. The section opens folded, with one verdict: Pass when every check passed, Fail as soon as one failed, Warning otherwise (a check that could not run counts as a warning). Click it for the details. A failed paternity check means another father, a sample mix-up, the father's own DNA in the plasma or more than one fetus (its message says which): do not read the variants.

Expected fetal reads is the QC gate: median target depth × FF/2, at least 40 (QA's bound, or the provisional 40 until QA sets it). Below it a fetal-specific allele may be missed, so a result without one is not reliable: consider a redraw. The sign-out then asks for a reason.

The filters sit under Advanced filters, closed when the page opens, as on the small-variant page. They are the small-variant page's Pathogenicity, Annotations, In silico, Frequency, Locations and Exclude filters and its review tags (Review and curation: the tags, not the classification or saved notes), plus Maternal/fetal categories (tick any of the eight; each shows its count), a minimum classification confidence, Hide recurrent low-VAF calls (below) and an Inheritance view: De novo in the fetus: calls in the fetal window without a supported call in the father, triaged and ranked by score. List de novo candidates of priority picks high, high and medium, or every candidate. Paternal, inherited by the fetus and Maternal, inherited by the fetus: each parent's alleles with the probability that the fetus inherited them. Also list the alleles the fetus did not inherit adds the rest. Recessive: both parents carriers: the genes where both parents carry an allele, and the X-linked genes read by the fetal sex (a son's mother's allele, one parent's allele of a daughter, each parent's when the sex is not known), each as a card as in the expanded carrier screen: which of its variants the fetus inherited (both, one of the two, neither), the pair that status rests on, and the fetal status with its probabilities. The status reads every carrier variant: the categories and Hide recurrent low-VAF calls choose which genes are listed, not their status.

De novo in the fetus: calls in the fetal window without a supported call in the father, triaged and ranked by score. List de novo candidates of priority picks high, high and medium, or every candidate.

Paternal, inherited by the fetus and Maternal, inherited by the fetus: each parent's alleles with the probability that the fetus inherited them. Also list the alleles the fetus did not inherit adds the rest.

Recessive: both parents carriers: the genes where both parents carry an allele, and the X-linked genes read by the fetal sex (a son's mother's allele, one parent's allele of a daughter, each parent's when the sex is not known), each as a card as in the expanded carrier screen: which of its variants the fetus inherited (both, one of the two, neither), the pair that status rests on, and the fetal status with its probabilities. The status reads every carrier variant: the categories and Hide recurrent low-VAF calls choose which genes are listed, not their status.

Each variant carries its category, the plasma reads, the father's genotype, the probabilities that the fetus inherited the paternal or maternal allele or is homozygous, a de novo candidate's priority, any flags and Other cfDNA samples: in how many other cfDNA samples of the assay, in every project, its allele is called, and how (maternal, the father's allele, or an unexplained low-VAF call that no parent explains, the mark of a recurrent artefact). This sits next to the usual annotation, tags and ACMG classification. As on the small-variant page, the diseases its gene is linked to are named under the card's heading, and Collapse folds a card you are done with to its heading.

Hide recurrent low-VAF calls leaves out the variants that are an unexplained low-VAF call in more than the number of other cfDNA samples you give. A variant that ClinVar may call pathogenic, or that is common in the population, stays listed, marked kept by the recurrence filter. The filter narrows the list only; the fetal fraction and the classifications do not change. The count grows with every pregnancy imported, so it is also how you find candidates for the assay's artifact list.

Download CSV, above the variants, saves the list as a CSV file: every variant the list classifies, in its order, with its category, reads, probabilities, de novo triage and recurrence, and on every row the fetal fraction and, for a multiple pregnancy, the multiple-pregnancy note. A list cut at its limit says so in the file name (TRUNCATED).

On-target coverage, under the variants, gives the median depth over the capture targets of the panel and genes you selected (every target without a selection) and how many genes have a weak target: a mean below 300× or a base without coverage, where a fetal variant can be missed. Coverage details opens the coverage page: the genes below target and above it, each opening to its targets and their depth. Back to NIPT returns to the NIPT page with your filters.

Read the probabilities, not only the category. A de novo or paternal allele shows clearly at any fetal fraction. Whether the fetus inherited a maternal allele needs depth and a fair fetal fraction: check its probability. An inheritance between 20% and 80% leaves a recessive gene's status undetermined, or not affected (carrier status undetermined) when the other allele surely did not reach the fetus. The recessive status assumes both alleles are pathogenic and, at two sites, in trans; an allele without a population frequency (every MNV) is noted.
Its footer names when it was made and the CoGA version that made it.
Its Scope names the panel and genes you selected; your other filters do not apply.
It lists up to 500 variants. When there are more, it says how many it lists of how many and where the list stops, on screen and in print. Narrow the scope with a panel or a gene.
An Import incomplete or Not validated for clinical use warning heads it, on screen and in print, whenever the family page would show one.
The report is live, never the signed record. It says so beside the latest signed version, and every printout starts with Draft or Not the signed report.
Tag the variants you report first. Show reported (N), in the NIPT page's header, lists them before you sign out: the variants tagged report, with every other filter cleared.

A tagged variant the analysis does not classify (not in the family's NIPT data, on the assay's artifact list, or without a call in the plasma) is in no list. The page names it above the list with the reason, as the signed record does.
Besides the Sample QC, a NIPT quality check that failed (no fetal-fraction estimate, fetal-sex signals that disagree, or male DNA as the maternal plasma) stops the sign-out until you record a reason.
Afterwards the signed version opens, with its report code. The NIPT report then shows Amend sign-out and says whether the data still matches the signed version.
Only a supervisor of the family's project, a superuser or an administrator signs out. For an analyst, a viewer or a reader the button is disabled, here and on the report, and says why.

Screening, not diagnosis. A NIPT call must be confirmed by an invasive diagnostic test. Check the fetal fraction and the quality checks before you read any variant, and a de novo candidate's absence in the father and its reads before you act on it.

conventional-nipt.title: Conventional NIPT
conventional-nipt.summary: Screen a pregnancy for aneuploidies and copy-number changes from the maternal plasma (ccnv): read the automatic result, its findings and its bounds.
paragraphs: A conventional NIPT screens a pregnancy for aneuploidies and copy-number changes from the genome-wide copy number of the maternal plasma. The laboratory's tool, ccnv, measures it; CoGA draws it and gives an automatic screening result per target. A high-risk result calls for confirmatory diagnostic testing; a low-risk result does not exclude an aneuploidy.

The validated claim covers trisomies 21, 18 and 13 and the sex-chromosome aneuploidies, in pregnancies of more than 12 weeks, singleton or twin. Triplets or more, a vanishing twin, a maternal organ or bone-marrow transplant or a blood transfusion in the months before sampling, and a known maternal malignancy are outside the validated scope. A twin pregnancy gets one result, which does not say which fetus a finding concerns.

A package import makes the family when its package says analysis_type: conventional_nipt (cNIPT in Deliveries) and names the pregnancy (pregnancy_id), with ccnv's bins, segments, calls and QC file for the plasma. A folder of ccnv output added by hand is read the same way: give its Pregnancy ID, and CoGA proposes the plasma as the mother of the pregnancy. The family page then shows a cNIPT tab.

A family may hold the NIPTs of several pregnancies of one woman, each an analysis of its own. A cNIPT and an mNIPT are one pregnancy only when their packages name the same pregnancy ID. The cNIPT page shows one pregnancy at a time: choose it in the analysis list beside the family name (conventional NIPT of pregnancy ZW1). The page opens on the pregnancy imported last. When the pregnancy's package lists two or more fetuses, the page, the report and the signed version show the multiple-pregnancy note: a fetal result may be present in one fetus or in more than one, and the analysis cannot tell which (not so for a monozygotic twin).

In the genome and chromosome views the plasma's track has an axis of its own. Each segment takes the colour of ccnv's call (purple where ccnv calls it discordant with the fetal fraction), and dashed lines mark where a fetal trisomy and monosomy lie at the fetal fraction.

Sign the family out from its Report page, which shows the result above the reported findings. The signed version keeps the result as the cNIPT page showed it, with the bounds and the files it was read from. A plasma without a result, a result on provisional bounds, or a result that could not be read at sign-out asks for an acknowledgement with a reason. When the family also holds another analysis (the monogenic NIPT of the pregnancy, or another pregnancy's NIPT), each is signed out on its own: the Report page signs out the conventional NIPT (of several pregnancies, the one you pick under Analysis to sign out; the button names it, Sign out the conventional NIPT of pregnancy ZW1), and its record freezes and checks that analysis's data only.
blocks: Setting up a conventional NIPT family

Result, headed with the plasma's sample ID, lists chromosomes 21, 18 and 13, the sex chromosomes and the segmental CNVs first, each High risk, Inconclusive, Low risk, No result or Not assessed, with why. When the fetal fraction is below ccnv's limit of detection of arm-level events, chromosomes 21, 18 and 13 and the sex chromosomes are Inconclusive rather than low risk. Another autosome is listed with them when it is not low risk; every autosome is under Every other autosome. The segmental CNVs and every autosome other than 21, 18 and 13 are marked outside the validated claim, here, on the report page and in the signed version: screen them as findings outside the claim.

Maternal plasma gives the fetal fraction the result uses (ccnv's effective one) and every other estimate, the fetal sex and the sex-chromosome call, the resolution (from which size segmental CNVs are assessed at this fetal fraction), and ccnv's warnings.

Findings, with their count, list every segment ccnv called and every segment in the grey zone, each with its size, log2 ratio, z-score, implied fetal fraction, origin and result. Click a region to open it in the chromosome view.

Bounds of the rule show the values the result applied. A bound QA has not set yet is marked provisional: provisional values are not validated. QA sets each bound in Admin → Sequencing QC thresholds, profile Conventional NIPT, each change with its reason.

explorers.title: Gene, variant and CNV explorers
explorers.summary: Questions beyond one case: a gene profile, a variant across the cohort, and the catalogue of clinical CNVs.
paragraphs: Three explorers answer questions beyond a single case. Open them from the menu under the arrow at the right of the top bar, or from the dashboard.

A profile per gene: the transcripts, badged MANE Select, MANE Plus Clinical, RefSeq Select and Ensembl Canonical; constraint metrics (pLI, LOEUF, missense constraint); disease associations with ClinGen and GenCC evidence and OMIM links; the Monarch gene–disease associations (see Phenotypes, panels and phenotype matching); and links to the main external resources.

Every small variant across the projects you can access, one row per variant: gene, variant, classification, consequence and tags, with the number of carriers (het and hom) and of families. A variant reviewed in more than one family shows the most severe classification of those reviews, and the tags of all of them. Each review counts with the class the family page shows for it, also when it holds only a class tag such as Likely pathogenic - class 4. Of two reviews of the same class, the row shows the one saved last. The classification filter keeps a variant one of whose reviews shows that class, as on the family page, so it also finds a review classified by its class tag alone. The row may show a more severe class, from another family's review.
The same filtered variants can also be viewed three other ways, from the tabs above the results:
The catalogue of known clinical CNVs (syndromes and recurrent regions) for an assembly. Search by name, chromosome or type; each row shows the CNV, cytoband, location, size and ClinVar P/LP.
blocks: ACMG secondary finding says whether the gene is on the ACMG secondary-findings list that CoGA ships: On ACMG SF v3.3, with the phenotype, category, inheritance, variants to report and footnotes the list gives for the gene, or Not on ACMG SF v3.3. Not checked means the list could not be read for this gene.

ClinGen dosage curation gives ClinGen's haploinsufficiency and triplosensitivity curations of the gene, the date of the curation and a link to ClinGen's report. The item with an HI score is ClinGen's haploinsufficiency score as dbNSFP carries it.
Filter as on the family page (gene, consequence, ClinVar, frequency, in-silico scores), plus tags and classification — for example every variant tagged Report.

The annotation filters work as on the family page: they must all hold on one transcript of the variant, one of the in-silico predictors you set is enough, and MANE only keeps nothing on GRCh37 or T2T (see Small-variant prioritisation).

Every filter is read for each family as its own family page reads it, so a row counts the carriers and families of the family pages that show the variant. When two families' files were annotated differently (two VEP runs), a filter on the gene, consequence, ClinVar or frequency counts only the family whose own annotation meets it.

A row counts only the samples their family shows. A member taken out of a family keeps its calls in that family's imported data, but is not counted there or listed among its carriers; the genotype filter neither offers nor reads a sample that no family shows.
A location reads the chromosome with or without chr, and the mitochondrion as chrM, M or MT.

Sample - genotype filter keeps the variants a sample carries as Het, Hom or Het + Hom (a haploid call, on chrM or a male's X, counts as hom). The row still counts every carrier in your projects, not only that sample's family.

A gene panel works as on the family page too: it keeps the variants of its genes and the variants in its regions (PanelApp's regions for the assembly, and each gene's position in the gene reference), so a variant whose annotation names its gene differently is kept. This holds for a panel of any size, the Mendeliome included.
Click a het, hom or family count to see the carriers per family, with links to their family pages.
Imputed calls are left out unless you tick Include imputed variants (GLIMPSE2 / SHAPEIT).

Download CSV exports the filtered variants with their annotation, up to 50,000 rows. Its Classification column holds the class the row shows, Classification text the classification as typed in the review that shows it. A file that misses matches has TRUNCATED in its name, and the page says why: more variants matched than the 50,000 rows (narrow the filters), or the tag or classification filter matched more than the 200,000 variants one search takes (filter on fewer tags or classifications).

The counts come from a summary CoGA keeps as families' variants are written. While a family is being imported, or for a few seconds after its members or projects change, the page says how many families are being added or brought up to date: their variants may be missing, or counted as before the change. Refresh in a moment.
A person sampled twice (two samples linked as the same individual) is one carrier, also when two families each show one of the samples. The carriers list still names each sample.
Each carrier counts once as heterozygous or homozygous: homozygous when any of the person's calls of the variant is, so the two counts add up to the carriers.

Genes: one row per gene a variant's annotation names, with the number of variants (also by their most severe impact on the gene) and the carriers summed over those variants: a sample with two variants in the gene counts twice. Click a gene to open its variants, where each variant's carriers are counted once.

Transcripts: one row per transcript a variant's annotation names, every transcript or only the MANE or canonical ones, with its gene and the variants by their most severe consequence on it (loss of function, missense or in-frame, splice region, synonymous, other) and the carriers summed over them. Click the gene to open its variants.

Cohort frequency: the variants by their number of carriers in your projects (1, 2–5, 6–20, 21–100, more than 100) against their gnomAD allele frequency (not in gnomAD, below 0.1 %, 0.1–1 %, 1–5 %, 5 % and more). Variants frequent here and rare in gnomAD can be artefacts or founder variants. Click a cell to open its variants; the filter shows above the results until you remove it.

Cytoband is the band the knowledgebase states. Where it states none, CoGA reads the bands the region spans from the assembly's cytobands, the ones the ideogram draws. An assembly without cytobands, such as T2T, shows none.

ClinVar P/LP, for example 12 loss · 3 gain, counts the pathogenic or likely pathogenic ClinVar copy-number variants that overlap the region by at least 30% both ways, as counted when the knowledgebase was built.
"—" means that the knowledgebase was built without ClinVar: not recorded, not zero.
Click a CNV for its detail page, with its description, the supporting ClinVar records and links to OMIM and DECIPHER. The same page opens when you click a clinical CNV in the viewers.
Counts follow your access. The variant explorer's cohort counts include only the projects you can see: your own, or every project for a superuser or an administrator.

administration.title: Administration
administration.summary: The admin dashboard: reference data, users and access, data management, variant configuration, database operations and audit logs.
paragraphs: Admin, in the top-bar menu, or Open admin dashboard on the dashboard opens the admin dashboard, grouped in six areas. A superuser sees five of its pages: Gene panels, Sequencing QC thresholds, Package import, Variant tags and Preset filters. Every other page is an administrator's alone.
blocks: Species & assemblies — the genome builds and their reference data (cytobands, genes, clinical CNVs, segmental duplications, DGV), with each dataset's status, and under ClinVar (CoGA) the current and the previous ClinVar release CoGA loaded for GRCh37 and GRCh38. Refresh the human gene information, rebuild the clinical-CNV knowledgebase, load the pinned DGV release or ClinVar's newest weekly release (Load newest), or upload a reference file. A ClinVar release becomes current only once its file matches NCBI's MD5, names its release and assembly, and is stored and counted whole; otherwise the page says why and the current release stays. Adding GRCh37 or GRCh38 starts the clinical-CNV build, the DGV load and the ClinVar load for it. CoGA holds one assembly per name: importing one it holds updates it in place (tick Replace existing cytobands and genes while it holds them), and Add assembly refuses a name that exists.

Gene panels — the panel catalogue: create panels, import them from PanelApp, and see their genes. A panel names each gene by its HGNC symbol or by its Ensembl gene ID (ENSG and eleven digits; a version such as .24 is dropped). The ID is the gene's stable name: a symbol can be renamed, or read as another gene's. A gene added by its ID is shown after its symbol, for example BRCA1 (ENSG00000012048), and the panel keeps its variants by the ID, by its symbol and by its position. Adding the ID of a gene the panel holds by its symbol replaces that symbol. A PanelApp search shows each panel's genes, regions and STRs by confidence level (green, amber, red). A panel can be imported green only, green + amber, or green + amber + red: each is a panel of its own, to filter on apart. An imported gene is kept by the Ensembl gene ID PanelApp gives it. Deleting a panel asks first, naming the panel and its version: its genes, its regions and every archived version go with it.

HPO terminology — the HPO release in use and the SHA-256 of the file it came from, and whether HPO has published a newer one; preview and apply a new release, downloaded from HPO or from a file on the server. The release is the one the file states. A file that states no release, or another than the release you asked for, is refused, and Apply imports only the file the preview showed. A new installation starts on HPO's newest release, downloaded at its first start; when HPO cannot be reached it starts on the release shipped with CoGA, which the page names.

Monarch data — load the Monarch release (gene–disease and disease–phenotype links) that powers phenotype matching and the ranking. A new installation loads the newest release at its first start; load a newer one about monthly. Loading it here also rebuilds the Mendeliome panel; after the first start, build that panel on the Gene panels page.

Repeat catalogue — each repeat locus with its cut-offs, which are STRchive's as the pinned release states them (the page names it, STRchive v2.28.0), what is known of TRGT's count there, and QA's count correction, with the reason, who and when, and the history of these corrections (a locus's disease links to its page on STRchive). The count correction, in repeats, is added to TRGT's count before every call at the locus is classified (−1 turns TRGT's 18 into 17; from −20 to 20), and TRGT's own count stays shown beside the corrected one. Set count correction changes it. No locus has one until QA enters it. At FMR1 a constant correction is wrong (TRGT is 1 to 3 low, by the number of AGG interruptions), and the page says so next to the field. A correction does not lift the Near a boundary mark, which the repeat page shows at every locus (Structural variants, repeats, Paraphase and mtDNA). Each change needs a reason and is kept in the clinical audit trail, with the record before and after. The loci the stored calls name are listed first.

Users — accounts, how each signs in (Microsoft or a password), roles and activation, and each user's projects with their level there (analyst or reader). A colleague's first Microsoft sign-in creates their account: a viewer in no project. Set an account's role in its Role list; each role's tooltip says what it may do. CoGA asks you to confirm; you cannot change your own. The roles, lowest first, each with every right of the ones before it: a viewer reads the records of their projects and changes none; an analyst also analyses them (reviews, tags, classifications, HPO terms, the case's workflow, new families); a supervisor also signs an analysis out; a superuser also has every project, member or not, and the gene panels, variant tags, preset filters, sequencing QC thresholds and package import; an admin has the whole administration. Give the supervisor role only to those the laboratory authorises to sign out. Each account shows when it was added and where it stands. A sign-up, or a first sign-in through the organisation, waits for approval: these accounts come first, and every active administrator gets an e-mail about each when a mail server is set (the page says who, and Send a test mail checks it). Activate the account, or Delete it when it is not relevant; only an account that was never active can be deleted. With a mail server set, an account you activate (or activate again) gets an e-mail that it can sign in. Deactivate an account to revoke access without deleting its history. Archive one that is not coming back: it is deactivated and leaves the list (tick Show archived accounts to see it), every record still names it, and the same person signing in again makes no new request. Restore brings it back, inactive. You cannot deactivate, archive or delete your own: another administrator does that. Edit, under Project access, sets the account's projects and its level in each: the same memberships as a project's members on Projects & access, set from the account's side. Remove takes a project off; Give access to a project lists a few projects without access at a time (type part of a name to find the others), and a project added starts as an analyst. The dialog lists what the save changes; Save project access saves it all at once. An administrator's or a superuser's row says it has every project, member or not. Every change asks you to confirm it first, and is kept in the audit log. When you deactivate an account, an import, a gene reference sync or a clinical CNV knowledgebase rebuild it asked for that has not started yet is not run, and a rebuild not yet loaded loads nothing: its job ends failed, saying why. The same holds once the account loses the role the job needs: superuser or administrator for an import (administrator for one that overwrites a family), administrator for the other two.

Projects & access — the projects (each tied to an assembly) and which families, samples and users belong to them. A user sees only the data of their projects; the cohort counts in the explorers follow the same scope. The members are listed with their level; Remove takes one off. Under them, Add a member lists a few users without access at a time: type part of a name or email to find the others, then Add one (or press Enter when the search finds one user). A member added starts as an analyst. One user's projects are also set on the Users page. An analyst reads the project's records and changes them as far as their role allows: a viewer changes nothing, whatever their level. A reader (a student, say) reads, searches, exports and prints them and saves their own filter presets, but changes nothing and does not see the audit trail. Superusers and administrators have every right in every project, member or not. A case can be assigned to, or reviewed by, an analyst of its projects whose role is not viewer, a superuser or an administrator. A case assigned to someone who became a reader or a viewer keeps them, marked (not eligible), until it is changed. A project that families are linked to cannot be deleted: Delete project is off and says how many. A family's small and structural variants are stored per project, and would stay behind under the deleted one. Deleting a project without families asks first and says what goes: its members lose the access it gave them; its review tags are deleted as a removed tag is: each stays on the reviews that hold it, marked deleted, and can no longer be added.

Family & sample data — the inventory of families and samples. A family's members are edited in its Family members table, the same as on the family page: Edit members, then Save changes (see Family workspace). A family's small and structural variants move with its projects: each project it is added to gets them, and a project it leaves no longer holds them. A project on another assembly than the family's variants is refused. Save project access waits while the family is being imported, and takes longer for a family with many variants. A deletion cannot be undone and is recorded in the audit log. Deleting a sample or a family is also written to the family's Clinical audit trail; a family's deletion is its last entry. Deleting a family asks for its name, typed out, and the reason it goes, which its last entry records. Without a reason it is not deleted. A data layer that more than one caller filled, such as a long-read sample's coverage from HiFiCNV, WisecondorX and QDNAseq, or its segments, lists each caller with its own Delete. Family statuses — the workflow statuses analysts give a case.

Sequencing QC thresholds — the warning and error cut-offs per assay behind the Seq. QC chip. None ship by default. Each metric of an analysis is judged by its warning and its error cut-off, each taken on its own from the analysis's own profile, else from the profile the family names, else from the default profile: a warning set alone in the analysis's profile keeps the default's error cut-off. The mtDNA QC is judged by the profile of the analysis whose import holds the mtDNA calls. A metric without a cut-off reads as not assessed, and a sample with no cut-off for any of its metrics shows Not run on the chip. The Conventional NIPT profile holds the bounds of the cNIPT result rule: until QA sets a bound there, with its reason, the rule applies its provisional value, which the cNIPT page, the report and the signed version mark provisional.
Package import — check, correct and approve the deliveries, and follow their imports (see Case setup and data import). A superuser imports too; only an administrator overwrites an existing family.

Variant tags — create, rename, recolour or remove custom review tags, for one project or for everyone. A renamed tag stays on every review and saved filter that uses it. A removed tag stays on the reviews that hold it, marked deleted, and can no longer be added. The built-in and ACMG tags are listed for reference.
Preset filters — the catalogue of the small-variant presets the team uses. Presets are saved on the small-variant page.

NIPT artefact list — the alleles that recur as an artefact in the cfDNA of one assay, one list per assembly and assay scope. Every monogenic NIPT analysis of the assay removes them, except an allele its annotation marks as more than 5% frequent or that ClinVar may call pathogenic, which stays in, flagged. Add an entry or remove one; Preview the auto-seed, the alleles that are an unexplained low-VAF call in at least the number of cfDNA samples you give (the preview writes nothing), then Seed the list; or Import the NIPT-M pipeline's table of recurrent artefacts. Every change is a clinical audit event on the list's own trail.

ClickHouse tables & operations — technical database maintenance, for the bioinformatics team. Each assembly shows the last result of the scheduled integrity check and when it ran; Integrity check runs one now.

Audit logs — every request to the server (who, what, when, the outcome) and every button and link a user clicked. Identifiers are masked, so the log shows how CoGA is used without exposing patient data. The Flags column marks: a request for a family, sample or project outside the user's projects, which CoGA answered as for an unknown one; a row in which a value the database cannot store was saved as an escape, naming the columns; an account made at its first Microsoft sign-in, or whose role or activation changed (from and to); every request of the emergency administrator's password sign-in (Emergency sign-in). The audit log is separate from each family's Clinical audit trail on the report.
